newsitem.title: USA: Cholesterol gene holds promise for heart disease.
newsitem.headline: Cholesterol gene holds promise for heart disease.

text.p: A newly discovered gene linked to a rare, lethal childhood ailment could help scientists learn how cholesterol acts in the development of heart disease, researchers reported on Thursday.

Scientists at the National Institutes of Health and other institutions have identified a mutation in a gene associated with Niemann-Pick type C (NPC) disease which kills children, usually before the age of 10, by blocking their absorption of so-called bad cholesterol.
This cholesterol then accumulates in the children's brains, livers, lungs, spleens and bone marrow, causing poor muscle control, impaired eye movements, slurred speech, dementia and death.
Only about 300 Americans have Niemann-Pick disease, and the chances of getting the inherited disorder are about one in a million, according to researcher Peter Pentchev.

The disease had been considered an epidemiological "orphan" -- so rare that funds to study it were scarce and enthusiasm by researchers was low -- but the identification of a gene governing the blockage of bad cholesterol is likely to open the floodgates for research into all kinds of cholesterol-related ailments, including heart attacks and strokes, Pentchev said in an interview.
The discovery was reported in the current edition of the journal Science.
NPC disease has a high-profile advocate in the United States: Ara Parseghian, the former head football coach at the University of Notre Dame whose three youngest grandchildren suffer from NPC.

"We can only win this fight by finding out why the gene acts why it does," Parseghian said in a statement. "And finally, we want to achieve the ultimate victory -- a cure for NPC. This is a race against time to save all children afflicted with this terrible disease."
Parseghian, whose grandson Michael died in March, four days before his 10th birthday, established a medical research foundation more than two years ago to study the disease.
In addition to Parseghian's foundation, researchers were aided by a bit of "divine intervention" in the form a spontaneously occurring mouse model of the NPC gene, Pentchev said.
Creating a mouse model would have taken three years or more. With the discovery of a model, tests on how the gene works on cholesterol can proceed more quickly, Pentchev said.

Mutations in the newly identified NPC1 gene have been linked with 95 percent of families where the disease is present, but the other 5 percent of families show no correlation, which means there must be another NPC gene, the scientists said.
There are dozens of other genes already identified with links to the absorption of bad cholesterol.
